title: A reliable distinction between early neoplasms that will kill and those that will not

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a clinically reliable way to estimate, at early diagnosis, whether a neoplasm would progress enough to harm or kill a person if left untreated. A biopsy or blood sample would provide information that helps distinguish lesions suitable for observation from lesions for which treatment offers a worthwhile benefit. The prediction would need a specified time horizon and clearly defined outcomes: leaving the organ, causing symptoms, and shortening life are distinct events, and a test that predicts one does not automatically predict the others. This is the target capability described by the supplied concept, not an established achievement.

Conceptual clarification: the title describes a distinction between lethal and nonlethal lesions, but a clinically usable implementation would ordinarily express calibrated risks and uncertainty rather than promise certainty about every lesion’s future. Its central purpose would be to make the decision between observation and treatment more reliable. Prediction of biological risk and evidence that acting on that prediction improves patient outcomes are related but separate requirements.

significance.text: Conditional significance: finding a small tumor does not by itself establish whether it will metastasize or shorten life. A sufficiently reliable classifier could change the consequences of early detection by allowing more people with low-risk lesions to avoid unnecessary treatment while preserving opportunities to intervene against dangerous disease. The direct advance would be better management decisions at diagnosis. Reduced overtreatment would follow only if clinicians and patients could safely change management on the basis of the result, with appropriate surveillance and access to treatment when needed.

Conditional downstream possibilities include fewer treatment complications, less treatment burden, and more selective use of clinical resources. Prostate cancer is the initial application emphasized in the research; extension to other screen-detected neoplasms would require separate validation. The supplied evidence does not establish that an indolent majority exists across all relevant cancers or quantify how many people could safely avoid treatment. Those proportions and benefits would depend on the cancer, screened population, prediction horizon, and management strategy.

An important limit is that classification does not cure dangerous lesions. Any survival benefit would also depend on effective local or systemic treatment and on treatment occurring early enough to help. The capability would inform the net benefit of screening, including ONC-01, but would not decide that benefit alone: detection performance, missed cancers, treatment effects, competing causes of death, and screening and treatment harms would still matter. The supplied material does not establish that risk classification is the single dominant limitation of screening.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability sought here is sufficiently accurate prediction of clinically consequential progression from information available while a lesion is still early. Scientific synthesis: a successful test would have to connect measurable pathology or molecular features to long-term outcomes, distinguish symptoms from metastasis and mortality, and specify how risk changes with time and competing mortality. The supplied record does not establish the present absence of every disease-specific version of this capability; it identifies the broader ambition and limitations of the reported supporting evidence.

A proposed biological and engineering barrier is obtaining a representative signal from limited material. A biopsy may fail to include a biologically important tumor population, while a blood-based implementation would need to show that an early lesion produces a detectable, interpretable signal. These are design concerns retained from, or inferred from, the proposed sampling approaches; their frequency and effect are not established by the supplied source excerpts, because no source texts were retained. A classifier would need to remain useful despite sampling variation, tumor heterogeneity, and possible evolution after diagnosis.

A further barrier is validating the right endpoint. Upgrading or upstaging can inform management, but prediction of those events is not equivalent to prediction of untreated metastasis or death. Whether a molecular score adds useful information beyond clinical variables must be tested for each cancer, population, and outcome. Methodological synthesis: validation must also confront the counterfactual problem that treating a lesion changes its course, so the outcome observed after treatment does not reveal what that same lesion would have done without treatment. Observation with later rescue treatment creates a similar distinction between validating a safe care strategy and identifying an entirely untreated natural history.

current_state.text: The research notes attribute to a 2025 European Urology pathology white paper, identified there by DOI 10.1016/j.eururo.2025.02.029, the conclusion that needle biopsy cannot reliably identify indolent prostate cancer. They also report that 22–27% of prostate cancers classified as grade group 1 on needle biopsy are upgraded at prostatectomy despite MRI-targeted and systematic biopsies. The supplied source index contains a URL but no retained text or document artifact, and does not establish the article title. These statements therefore remain attributed reports: the exact wording, population, biopsy procedures, denominator, and numerical context could not be checked in the supplied review. If confirmed, the upgrading rate would describe disagreement between biopsy and prostatectomy grading in the studied population, not the proportion of lesions destined to kill.

The research also attributes to Braun AE and colleagues in Cancer in 2024, DOI 10.1002/cncr.35215, clinical-model AUCs of 0.70 and 0.69 in two favorable-risk prostate cancer cohorts for predicting upgrading or upstaging. It reports an AUC of 0.72 after adding a genomic classifier and characterizes the incremental improvement as limited. These quantitative details are preserved as reported, but no retained source text or artifact was available to verify the cohort definitions, endpoint construction, uncertainty estimates, or which comparison produced the combined-model result. AUC measures discrimination for the studied endpoint; these figures alone would not establish accurate absolute risks, a useful treatment threshold, or prediction of untreated lethality.

The research additionally states that genomic assays already inform some decisions about adjuvant treatment intensity, but the supplied material does not provide inspectable support sufficient to establish which assays, cancers, or decisions are meant. Even if confirmed, that use would be a distinct achievement from determining which untreated early neoplasms will cause death. The available account concerns reported findings from 2024–2025; the supplied review contains no later freshness evidence sufficient to establish the state of the capability as of November 1, 2026. Missing retained evidence limits verification and does not show that the reported findings are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: begin with a screen-detected cancer in which substantial overtreatment is established, define the intended population and prediction horizon, and lock the classifier and decision thresholds before prospective evaluation. Within the group proposed for observation, a randomized comparison of observation against immediate definitive treatment should demonstrate noninferior cancer-specific survival using a prespecified, clinically acceptable margin and adequate follow-up. Surveillance schedules, triggers for reassessment, rescue-treatment rules, and handling of crossovers should be explicit. These are proposed criteria for convincing evidence, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Observation demonstrates noninferior cancer-specific survival versus immediate definitive treatment

completion_criteria.text: The complementary group would need evidence of both consequential risk and sufficient expected treatment benefit to justify intervention; a high predicted risk alone would not establish that treatment helps. Proposed evaluation should separately report metastasis, symptoms, cancer-specific mortality, overall mortality, treatment complications, and the proportion initially observed who later require treatment. It should assess calibrated risk estimates as well as discrimination, and report uncertainty and clinically consequential classification errors. The required sample size and follow-up would depend on event rates, the chosen survival margin, and the natural history of the cancer.
completion_criteria.label: Intervention group shows consequential risk and sufficient expected treatment benefit

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent cohorts and clinical settings should reproduce the classifier’s performance and the benefit of its management strategy, with reproducible sample processing, pathology interpretation, and assay results. Validation should define where performance is reliable across patient groups, specimen quality, and lesion characteristics, and where results remain uncertain. Replication in a second early-neoplasm type would broaden the demonstrated scope, but further cancers would still require validation. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth and safe management within defined conditions; they would not prove literal universality or reveal every treated lesion’s untreated fate.
completion_criteria.label: Independent cohorts reproduce classifier performance and management strategy benefit

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ONC-01, mortality-reducing detection of lethal cancers while they are still localized, is the closest complement. ONC-01 concerns finding dangerous disease early enough to reduce mortality; ONC-10 concerns interpreting an early lesion’s risk and choosing management. Better classification could make early detection more useful, while neither capability alone establishes the other. ONC-08, interception of non-viral precancers before they invade, overlaps in identifying lesions that warrant intervention, but its defining achievement is prevention of invasion through interception. ONC-09, prophylactic immunity against common non-viral cancers, acts earlier through prevention and would remain distinct from classifying an existing lesion.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-02, sterilizing immune clearance of established metastatic carcinomas, and ONC-03, eradication of dormant disseminated tumor cells responsible for late relapse, concern treatment after malignant cells have spread. ONC-10 could help identify early lesions at risk of producing such disease, but it would neither clear established metastases nor eradicate dormant cells. Successful early-risk classification would also not establish that dissemination has never occurred.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-04, a shared malignant dependency that renewing normal tissues can spare, and ONC-05, therapies that drive the whole clonal population to extinction, address therapeutic selectivity and completeness. Tumor heterogeneity is relevant to ONC-10 because limited samples may omit important populations; in ONC-05, the concern is whether treatment eliminates all populations capable of sustaining disease. ONC-06, stable reversion of carcinoma cells to non-malignant tissue identity, changes malignant behavior rather than predicting it. These treatment advances could help patients assigned to a dangerous-risk group without replacing the need for reliable classification.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-07, body-wide delivery that alters essentially every malignant cell, addresses therapeutic reach. ONC-11, real-time, cell-resolution guidance that makes incomplete cancer surgery uncommon, addresses surgical completeness. ONC-12, off-the-shelf cell therapy that matches autologous cures at ordinary scale, addresses therapeutic efficacy and availability. Each could improve outcomes after a decision to treat, whereas ONC-10 addresses whether and when treatment is justified. Their achievements would require separate demonstrations.

change_log.reason: Metastasis, symptoms, and shortened life are distinct endpoints; the original binary framing needed an operational explanation without implying certainty or achievement.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad claim that current molecular scores add little with a cancer-, population-, and endpoint-specific assessment.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence cannot support a general conclusion about molecular scores across early neoplasms.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 22–27% upgrading rate and AUCs of 0.70, 0.69, and 0.72 with explicit attribution and verification limits.
change_log.reason: The source index contains no retained texts or artifacts. Preserving the figures as reported avoids treating either unverified claims as established findings or missing evidence as disproof.

change_log.change: Separated upgrading, upstaging, and adjuvant decision support from prediction of untreated lethality.
change_log.reason: These outcomes and uses do not independently demonstrate the proposed capability.

change_log.change: Replaced equal survival with a proposed noninferiority design, including a prespecified margin, follow-up, surveillance, and rescue-treatment rules.
change_log.reason: A convincing comparison needs an operational survival criterion and an explicit account of later treatment.

change_log.change: Added the need to establish treatment benefit in the complementary high-risk group and distinguished management validation from individual untreated fate.
change_log.reason: Risk alone does not establish treatment benefit, and outcomes altered by treatment do not directly reveal an untreated counterfactual.

change_log.reason: Those claims exceed the supplied evidence; screening benefit also depends on detection, effective treatment, competing mortality, and harms.

change_log.reason: Finite validation cannot establish unrestricted generality across early neoplasms.

unresolved_issues: Neither listed source has retained text or artifacts. Document identity, exact passages, study populations, quantitative context, and uncertainty estimates remain unverified.
The supplied material does not identify the assays or clinical settings supporting the statement about adjuvant treatment-intensity decisions.
Evidence sufficient to establish the capability’s present scope or remaining absence as of November 1, 2026 is not supplied.
The appropriate initial cancer, prediction horizon, acceptable noninferiority margin, follow-up duration, and treatment thresholds remain to be specified and justified.
The frequency and clinical effect of missing consequential tumor populations in biopsy samples, and the feasibility of an early-lesion blood signal, remain unestablished here.
A classifier-guided strategy could demonstrate safe management without resolving every lesion’s untreated fate; the extent to which that stronger individual-level ambition is achievable remains open.
The review’s concern that ONC-01 was undefined was resolved only to the extent permitted by the supplied roster title; detailed technical overlap cannot be assessed from that title alone.

brief.title: Knowing which early tumors need treatment
possible: If a small tumor were found during screening, you could get a reliable estimate of whether it would harm you if left untreated. A biopsy, a small tissue sample, or a blood sample could help you and your doctor choose between monitoring and treatment.
The estimate would describe your risk over a defined period. It would distinguish a tumor causing symptoms, spreading beyond its organ, and shortening your life.
why: More people with low-risk tumors could avoid unnecessary treatment and its complications. People with dangerous tumors could receive treatment while it can still help.
Prostate cancer is the first application proposed. Better decisions could reduce the burden of treatment on patients and focus clinical resources on people likely to benefit.

sources.who: Authors of the European Urology pathology white paper
sources.showed: This is a pathology white paper about the limits of identifying slow-growing prostate cancer from needle biopsies.
sources.cited_for: It reports that needle biopsies cannot reliably identify prostate cancers that will remain harmless.
sources.not_established: Differences between biopsy findings and findings after surgery do not establish which untreated tumors would cause death.

sources.showed: This is a study of clinical prediction models and a test based on genetic information in people with apparently low-risk prostate cancer.
sources.cited_for: It supports the limited added value of genetic information for predicting more aggressive or extensive disease.
sources.not_established: Predicting more aggressive or extensive disease does not establish the risk of death without treatment or the benefit of treatment.

shown: Braun AE and colleagues assessed predictions of whether apparently low-risk prostate cancers would prove more aggressive or extensive. Adding a test based on genetic information reportedly gave limited improvement. This falls short of predicting which untreated tumors would shorten life.
missing: A test must reliably connect information from an early tumor to its long-term risk of symptoms, spread and death.
Results must remain useful when samples miss important parts of a tumor or the tumor changes after diagnosis.
Trials must establish that test-guided monitoring preserves survival and that treatment benefits those selected for it.

milestones.label: Monitoring preserves survival compared with immediate treatment
milestones.explanation: A randomized trial would have to show that monitoring the group selected by the test causes no unacceptable loss of cancer-specific survival. This would establish whether those patients can safely defer treatment.

milestones.label: Patients selected for treatment have risk and expected benefit
milestones.explanation: The treatment group would need evidence of consequential disease risk and enough expected treatment benefit to justify its harms. This would establish that the test identifies people worth treating.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce predictions and benefits of care
milestones.explanation: Independent patient groups and care settings would have to reproduce the test's performance and the benefit of using it. This would establish where the approach works reliably and define its limits.

uncertain: The appropriate cancer, prediction period, treatment threshold and acceptable survival difference remain to be defined.
It remains unclear whether early tumors release a blood signal that can reliably reveal their future danger.
Safe monitoring with later treatment may be demonstrable even when an individual tumor's entirely untreated future remains unknowable.

page.title: Prognostic stratification of early neoplasms
page.definition: Tests at diagnosis estimate an early neoplasm’s risks of symptoms, metastasis (spread to distant sites), and cancer-specific death over a stated interval without immediate treatment. They identify candidates for observation; outcomes under surveillance with later treatment do not establish the lesion’s entirely untreated lifetime course.

goal.need: ProtecT randomized 1,643 men with localized prostate cancer. After a median of 15 years, 133 men assigned to active monitoring were alive without prostate cancer treatment. Metastasis and cancer-specific death occurred at different frequencies. Selecting treatment deferral requires prognosis that distinguishes these outcomes and accounts for subsequent treatment.

figures.caption: ProtecT outcomes after a median of 15 years of follow-up, published on 11 March 2023.
figures.note: Active monitoring allowed subsequent treatment. These are randomized management outcomes, not risks under lifelong absence of treatment.

completion.title: Test-guided observation reduces treatment and meets a registered cancer-mortality safety criterion.
completion.criterion: For one defined neoplasm and patient population, a fixed diagnostic test independently validates absolute cancer-specific mortality risk under an explicit policy without immediate definitive treatment. In a prospective comparison, test-guided care reduces definitive treatment and meets the registered protocol’s noninferiority criterion for cancer-specific mortality, with metastasis assessed separately. The protocol supplies the decision threshold, margin and follow-up. This validates a management policy, not an individual lesion’s never-treated lifetime fate.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no outside body’s completion standard for the combined capability was identified.
completion.basis: NCI’s programme goals, GUPS/ISUP’s white paper, ASCO’s guideline, IOM’s validation framework, and COMET/G-MAJOR protocols were searched for a completion standard. No common accuracy, follow-up or excess cancer-mortality threshold was found. Prolaris supplies an indication-specific risk cutoff. The criterion combines independently validated prognosis with clinical utility for one indication, using protocol-defined limits.

milestones.title: A prognostic assay meets its analytical acceptance criteria on its intended specimen type.
milestones.criterion: The assay and calculation meet intended-use analytical acceptance limits on representative specimens, including precision, accuracy and reproducibility. The 2013 Genomic Prostate Score study tested 10 RNA samples: precision and reproducibility standard deviations were 1.86 and 2.11 points on its 100-point scale. The 2023 DCISionRT study tested 15 specimens of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS; neoplasia confined to breast ducts); its algorithmic score standard deviation was 0.20 on a 10-point scale under varied laboratory conditions.
milestones.set_by: Institute of Medicine committee, Evolution of Translational Omics (2012), Chapter 3. Acceptance limits depend on the assay and intended use; the committee supplies no universal numerical cutoff.
milestones.threshold_quote: The test method should be optimized to achieve an analytically validated test, including the assay and the fully specified computational procedures.

milestones.title: A fixed prognostic test reproduces its outcome association in an independent patient cohort.
milestones.criterion: A fixed assay reproduces its prognostic association in a separate, clinically comparable cohort using the same endpoint. Prostate: a 2015 independent cohort of 585 conservatively managed men validated cancer-death prediction. Myriad’s surveillance threshold corresponds to 3.2% estimated 10-year mortality (95% CI 2.0–5.2). Breast DCIS: 327 women after excision without radiotherapy validated recurrence prediction in 2013; low-score 10-year invasive recurrence was 3.7%. This is postoperative risk. Braun’s 2024 clinical models in 864/2,267 men predicted upgrading/upstaging, with areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.70/0.69.
milestones.set_by: Simon–Paik–Hayes archived-specimen validation criteria (2009), incorporated into the Institute of Medicine’s 2012 evaluation framework. Each indication retains its own endpoint and decision threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: the results from archived specimens should be validated using specimens from one or more similar, but separate, studies.

milestones.title: Test-informed management improves a patient outcome in a prospective comparative trial.
milestones.criterion: A prospective comparative trial meets its prespecified patient-outcome endpoint. Related breast evidence: COMET randomized 957 women with hormone-receptor-positive, grade 1–2 DCIS. At 2 years, same-breast invasive diagnoses were 4.2% with monitoring versus 5.9% with guideline-concordant care; the difference’s 95% upper confidence bound was 0.95 percentage points, below the 5-point margin. Monitoring included endocrine therapy in 345/484 women. This tested clinicopathologic eligibility, not a molecular assay. Prostate: G-MAJOR compares immediate with delayed genomic-result disclosure.
milestones.set_by: ASCO’s Molecular Biomarkers in Localized Prostate Cancer guideline (2020), supported by IOM’s general clinical-utility framework (2012). ASCO’s recommendation is prostate-specific; COMET’s numerical margin is DCIS-specific.
milestones.threshold_quote: have not been prospectively tested or shown to improve long-term outcomes—for example, quality of life, need for treatment, or survival.

results.finding: Oncotype DX prostate assay: 10 prostate tumor RNA samples had a GPS precision standard deviation of 1.86 points on a 100-point scale.
results.detail: All prespecified analytical criteria were met. GPS reproducibility SD was 2.11 points; individual gene assay accuracy met its prespecified limits.
results.quote:
The estimates of analytical precision and reproducibil-
ity were obtained by analyzing 10 prostate tumor RNA
samples on multiple instruments, using multiple reagent
lots, by various operators over a period of 2 weeks.
Standard deviation for precision for the analytical
process was at or below 0.21 Cp for all gene assays and
1.86 GPS units on a 100 unit scale.

results.finding: DCISionRT algorithmic scores for 15 DCIS specimens had a standard deviation of 0.20 on a 10-point scale.
results.detail: The score SD was below the stated target of 0.4 under varied antibody lots, machines and run days. Molecular assays also showed at least 95% concordance for the reported sensitivity, specificity and available inter-laboratory comparisons.
results.quote: The overall standard deviation of the dispersion of the mean over replicates under controlled non-standard conditions was low (0.20/10 point scale), and the analytic variables Lot, Machine and Run accounted for (<1%) of the total variance on average, where the DS confidence interval was (95%CI: -0.4, 0.4) on a 10-point scale.

results.finding: In 585 men with localized prostate cancer, the CCP score predicted prostate cancer death (hazard ratio 2.08 per unit).
results.detail: The cohort was independent and initially managed conservatively. Subsequent treatment was incompletely documented; outcomes do not establish the entirely untreated course.
results.quote: In univariate analysis, the CCP score hazard ratio was 2.08 (95% CI (1.76, 2.46), Po10 /C0 13) for one unit change of the score.

results.finding: In 585 conservatively managed men with prostate cancer, a fixed CCR threshold predicted 10-year prostate cancer mortality (p=0.00080).
results.detail: The threshold was selected in a separate training cohort. The validation cohort had previously been used to validate the CCR model, but not the threshold; it included relatively few low-risk men.

results.finding: In 571 patients with DCIS, the DCIS Score predicted local recurrence in an independent cohort (HR 2.15 per 50 score units).
results.detail: The prespecified assay and recurrence endpoint were evaluated after breast-conserving surgery alone, with negative margins. The cohort was more diverse than the original low-risk cohort; this is postoperative risk.

results.finding: In 78 women with DCIS treated without radiotherapy, DCISionRT score was associated with total breast event risk (HR 2.70 per 5 score units).
results.detail: This was an independent validation using a predetermined algorithm. Outcomes followed breast-conserving surgery; the no-radiotherapy subgroup analysis was exploratory and included some patients prescribed endocrine therapy.

results.finding: COMET analyzed 957 women with low-risk DCIS; the upper confidence bound for the 2-year invasive cancer risk difference was 0.95 percentage points.
results.detail: The bound was below the prespecified 5-point noninferiority margin. Eligibility used clinicopathologic features, not a molecular assay. Endocrine therapy was used by 345 of 484 women in the monitoring group; longer-term outcomes remain uncertain.
